name: Ghadames Berber
confidence_why: Kossmann 2013, the only modern description (known through Heath 2016's review and Kossmann's own 2000 footnote), says little is known about Ghadames accent beyond reading Lanfry's vowel-length marks as accent on full vowels, and Lanfry 1973 himself wrote that he could not tell a long syllable from an accented one, so no source offers a placement rule and none contradicts the undetermined classification, but everything rests on one fieldworker's pre-1945 data and one reanalysis read at second hand.
catalog_citation: Kossmann, Maarten. 2013. A Grammatical Sketch of Ghadames Berber (Libya). Berber Studies 40. Cologne: Rüdiger Köppe, §2.4 Accent, p. 18 (and p. 104) — as reported in Heath, Jeffrey. 2016. Review of Maarten Kossmann, A grammatical sketch of Ghadames Berber (Libya). Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 37(1): 161-163. DOI 10.1515/jall-2016-0005
catalog_quote: Kossmann's main transcriptional adjustment is to reinterpret Lanfry's "wildly vacillating notations of vowel length" (18) as accent on full ("plain") vowels {i e a o u}. He confesses that "little is known" about the accentual system (18). Lanfry's cases of double accent like énér 'oil lamp' remain unexplained. / This issue reappears where the locative "clitic" results in contrasts like táli 'room' versus locative tálí 'in the room' (104). Elsewhere the locative is realized segmentally as = (y)i. Perhaps tálí is really talí < /táli = yi/ parallel to e. g. locative almudú 'in a mosque' from almúdu 'mosque' (104).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ghadames Berber has a word accent (realised as vowel length in Lanfry's notation) that falls on a full vowel (i, e, a, o, u), never on the short central vowels; the primary description (Kossmann 2013: 18) is reported to say that little is known about its placement. Lanfry's own glossary shows accent placement distinguishing aspect stems (aorist íkṣəḍ vs preterite ikṣə́ḍ, p. 169) and Kossmann's data show a locative accent shift (táli vs tálí), i.e. placement is lexically/morphologically determined rather than given by a phonological position rule. No positional rule is stated in any source opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; Heath notes Lanfry's unexplained 'double accent' words such as énér 'oil lamp'.
new_statements.exceptions: Double-accent words (énér); accent shift with the locative (táli 'room' vs tálí 'in the room', Kossmann 2013: 104); Lanfry 1973: 169 marks aspect stems by accent position ('exceptionnellement des accents').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms in Lanfry's glossary, texts collected before 1945 among the Ayt Waziten of Ghadames). Kossmann 2000: 252 n. 1 (first-hand, held by the project) adds that Lanfry's 'long vowels' are probably 'un allongement causé par l'accent ou par des assimilations'.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Ghadames oasis variety (glottocode ghad1239), specifically the parler of the Ayt Waziten quarter (Lanfry's informants; Kossmann 2013 is a reanalysis of Lanfry's material); Motylinski's 1904 informant was from the Ayt Wälid quarter. Prasse (EB 1998) treats these as two groups of quarter dialects of one language.

new_statements.quote: p. 169, no. 0830 KSD: "La notation qui a été plusieurs fois vérifiée, porte exceptionnellement des accents : l'aoriste : iksad, accent sur première syllabe ; le prétérit : iksad, accent sur la deuxième." — p. 188, no. 0942 LZ: "Pas d'opposition vocalique entre a. et prêt. ; mais on a noté un accent avant 1re rad. à l'a. et accent entre 1re et 2e rad. au prêt. Il semble que la remarque soit valable pour plusieurs verbes de la série 4 b." — p. 125, no. 0575 H uhu: "On a noté un accent sur la première voyelle. Elle est sans aucun doute accentuée. Est-elle longue en même temps ? Elle peut l'être par procédé expressif. Mais, si on dit uhù, avec accent et allongement de la deuxième syllabe, la nuance est : pas question, il n'y a pas moyen."
new_statements.translation: p. 169: "The notation, which was checked several times, exceptionally carries accents: the aorist: iksad, accent on the first syllable; the preterite: iksad, accent on the second." — p. 188: "No vocalic opposition between aorist and preterite; but an accent was noted before the 1st radical in the aorist and between the 1st and 2nd radical in the preterite. The remark seems to hold for several verbs of series 4 b." — p. 125: "An accent was noted on the first vowel. It is without any doubt accented. Is it long at the same time? It can be, by expressive means. But if one says uhù, with accent and lengthening of the second syllable, the nuance is: out of the question, no way."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Heath 2016 / Kossmann 2013 statement that Lanfry's length marks encode accent and that little is known: Lanfry's own entries confirm that he could not separate length from accent, and add the observation that in several verb series the aorist carries accent on the first syllable and the preterite on the second. The catalog record for the language has an empty rule; nothing here supplies a fixed placement. Note that the opened scan is vol. II (1973 Glossaire, pp. 1-223), not vol. I (1968), whose phonetic notes (pp. XXXIV sqq.) remain unopened; archive.org advancedsearch lists only the three vol. II scans and HathiTrust has no record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lanfry gives no accent rule anywhere in the opened text; the transcription system section (vol. II pp. XII-XVII) only refers back to vol. I p. XXXIV sq. for vowels and is silent on accent. In scattered entries he records accent only where it distinguishes verb stems: aorist with accent on the first syllable versus preterite with accent on the second (idad/idad, iksad/iksad, laz-type series 4 b verbs), and an accented first vowel in the negation uhu versus expressive uhù. Accent placement thus varies with morphology (verb theme) and Lanfry himself cannot separate accent from vowel length.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent marks are written only 'exceptionnellement', where the aorist/preterite opposition rests on accent alone (series 4 b verbs: dad, laz, san, zan; KSD); expressive lengthening/accent on the second syllable of uhù.
new_statements.identity_note: Lanfry's glossary (vol. II, Avant-propos p. IV) describes only the dialect of the Ayt Waziten quarter of Ghadames, with occasional notes on the Elt Ulid / Ayt Mazizen variety; the transcription is that of vol. I.

tone_statements.quote: The Berber – now known as Amazigh – languages are all non-tonal but appear to vary regarding presence of stress. The Eastern varieties (in Tunisia, Libya and Egypt) display word-level stress (Kossmann 2012), though without stress minimal pairs. Relatively little is known about the word prosody of most Libyan dialects, such as Ghadames (Kossmann 2013), but in Zwara stress generally falls on the penult (Gussenhoven 2017).

tone.quote: Berber languages of Morocco and Algeria (except Tuareg) do not seem to have a system of word accent. Instead, accentual features are governed by higher level prosodic organization, which one could call intonation. The situation is different in the Berber languages of Libya and Egypt, and in Tuareg.
